# R1 Digest — Preface + Introduction (raw 221–1038)
**Source:** Hamilton, *The Book of Genesis: Chapters 1–17* (NICOT 1990)
**Coverage:** slice lines 1–818 read in full (= raw lines 221–1038). Content verified: Author’s Preface, Publisher’s Note, Introduction §§I–VII (Title, Structure, Composition, Theology, Problems in Interpretation, Canonicity, Hebrew Text). Bibliography begins after this range — not read; no biblio content invented.
**Extractor note:** Subagent extraction only; no wiki writes. All interpretive claims attributed to Hamilton.

## Claims

### C-V1R1-01 | Preface — invitation and hesitation
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Hamilton accepted the NICOT Genesis commentary at R. K. Harrison’s invitation and Dennis Kinlaw’s encouragement, despite many existing “opus magnum” Genesis commentaries (Gunkel, Skinner, von Rad, Westermann).
- **Quote:** "I would like to express my appreciation to Professor Emeritus R. K. Harrison of Wycliffe College, University of Toronto, for his invitation to write the Genesis commentary for the NICOT series… As one colleague put it to me, rather laconically, “How much more juice can be squeezed from the lemon?”"
- **Locus:** slice L3–6 / raw L223–226; Author’s Preface
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]]

### C-V1R1-05 | Title — Genesis / berē’šîṯ
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** The English title “Genesis” comes via Latin Vulgate from Greek LXX *Génesis*, best rendered “origin”; postbiblical Hebrew titles the book *berē’šîṯ*, the first word of 1:1, following Pentateuchal first-word naming custom.
- **Quote:** "The title “Genesis” comes to us by way of the Latin Vulgate… which in turn borrowed, or transliterated, from the Greek LXX, Génesis. This word is best reproduced in English by “origin.” In postbiblical Hebrew usage the title is berē’ šîṯ, which is, in fact, simply the first word of 1:1 (“In [the] beginning”)."
- **Locus:** slice L52–54 / raw L272–274; Introduction §I Title
- **Targets:** [[genesis]]

### C-V1R1-06 | Title — medieval alternate Hebrew names
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Some medieval Hebrew MSS and commentators used titles such as “First Book,” “Book of the Creation of the World,” “Book of the Righteous,” *Sepher ha-B’riah* / *Sepher ha-Yetsirah* (Abrabanel; Nahmanides), and “Book of Yashar” (Midrash Habiur, because of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob as the righteous).
- **Quote:** "Some Hebrew manuscripts from the Middle Ages used titles like “First Book,” “Book of the Creation of the World,” and “Book of the Righteous.”"
- **Locus:** slice L56 / raw L276
- **Targets:** [[genesis]], [[abraham]]

### C-V1R1-07 | Title — origins without theogony
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Genesis is concerned with origins (earth’s creation, humankind, institutions, one chosen family as medium of world blessing), but transcending these is God, who has no *génesis theoú* (theogony) and no beginning or end.
- **Quote:** "There is no génesis theoú (theogony) in Scripture’s introductory book, nor any theobiography. He is one without rē’šîṯ (beginning) and ’aharîṯ (end)."
- **Locus:** slice L58 / raw L278
- **Targets:** [[genesis]], [[creation-ex-nihilo]]

### C-V1R1-08 | Structure — ten ’ēlleh tôlĕdôt formulae
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Few biblical books show unit demarcation as clearly as Genesis, because of the formula *’ēlleh tôlĕdôt* used ten times; translation preference (“story/history of X” vs. “descendants/generations of X”) depends on whether narrative or genealogy follows.
- **Quote:** "Few books of Scripture reveal the lines of demarcation between their individual units as clearly as does Genesis. This is due to the presence of the formula ’ēlleh ṯôleḏôṯ, used ten times throughout Genesis."
- **Locus:** slice L68 / raw L288; Introduction §II Structure
- **Targets:** [[genesis]], [[toledot]]

### C-V1R1-09 | Structure — list of ten tôlĕdôt occurrences
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** The ten occurrences are at 2:4a (heavens and earth); 5:1a (Adam); 6:9a (Noah); 10:1a (sons of Noah); 11:10a (Shem); 11:27a (Terah); 25:12a (Ishmael); 25:19a (Isaac); 36:1a, 9a (Esau); 37:2a (Jacob).
- **Quote:** "The ten are (and we translate “generations” only for continuity):1. 2:4a: “these are the generations of the heavens and the earth” … 10. 37:2a: “these are the generations of Jacob”"
- **Locus:** slice L69–105 / raw L289–325
- **Targets:** [[toledot]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[adam]], [[abraham]]

### C-V1R1-10 | Structure — five narrative vs five genealogical headings
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Five formulae are followed by narrative (creation, flood, Abraham, Jacob, Joseph stories) and should read “this is the story of X”; five head genealogies (Adam, sons of Noah, Shem, Ishmael, Esau).
- **Quote:** "in five of them the formula is followed by narrative: #1 (creation), #3 (the flood), #6 (Abraham story), #8 (Jacob story), #10 (Joseph story). In these five the introductory note should read “this is the story of X.”"
- **Locus:** slice L111 / raw L331
- **Targets:** [[toledot]], [[genesis]], [[abraham]]

### C-V1R1-11 | Structure — vertical vs horizontal genealogies
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Vertical (linear) genealogies: Adam→Noah (5:1ff.) and Shem→Abraham (11:10ff.), each ten generations ending with a father of three sons; horizontal/segmented: Shem/Ham/Japheth (10:1), Ishmael’s twelve (25:12), Esau (36:1, 9)—these last three barely protrude into narrative.
- **Quote:** "One type is the vertical genealogy, which traces one line of descent. … The second type of genealogy in Genesis is a horizontal or segmented type in which the genealogy is not traced through one son (the oldest), but through various children."
- **Locus:** slice L113–121 / raw L333–341
- **Targets:** [[toledot]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[abraham]]

### C-V1R1-12 | Structure — 2:4a superscript not subscript (preferred)
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Against majority modern versions/BHK/BHS that treat 2:4a as subscript to 1:1–2:3, Hamilton prefers 2:4a as introduction to what follows (2:4bff.), and argues all *tôlĕdôt* formulae should be read as titles, not conclusions.
- **Quote:** "It is equally arguable that 2:4a is an introduction to what follows. This is our preference… Does the first of these structure-providing formulae conclude what has just been recounted, or does it introduce what follows?"

### C-V1R1-13 | Structure — problems if 2:4a is P subscript on Yahwistic continuation
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Tacking 2:4a onto 1:1–2:3 while holding Priestly (1:1–2:3) vs Yahwistic (2:4bff.) creation stories creates an almost insurmountable problem, because elsewhere the formula is almost universally a superscript; von Rad’s special pleading for a Priestly interpolator is “strained.”
- **Quote:** "an almost insurmountable problem is created if one tacks on 2:4a to 1:1-2:3, and yet wishes to hold on to Priestly (1:1-2:3) and Yahwistic (2:4bff.) creation stories. Almost all commentators agree… that the phrase in question functions everywhere else in Genesis as a superscript."

### C-V1R1-14 | Structure — *tôlĕdôt* means offspring of X, not generation of X
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Because the formula is always followed by “the genitive of the progenitor, never of the progeny,” 2:4a refers to what the heavens and earth generate (man and woman in 2:5ff.), not to the generation of the heavens and earth themselves—so only as superscription.
- **Quote:** "since the formula is always followed by “the genitive of the progenitor, never of the progeny,” the phrase can only refer to that which is generated by the heavens and the earth, and not to the generation of the heavens and the earth themselves."

### C-V1R1-15 | Structure — 1:1–2:3 and 2:4ff. as complementary poles
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** 2:4ff. forms a polarity/*kenegdô* complement with 1:1–2:3: ch. 1 stresses divine image, endowments, authority (“you shall,” 1:29); 2:4ff. stresses mundane origins and creation under authority (“you shall not,” 2:17); neither is more truthful or important than the other.
- **Quote:** "Just as 1:1-2:3 focus on humanity’s divine origins and endowments, so 2:4ff. focus on humanity’s mundane origins. For this reason 1:1-2:3 draws our attention to a primal couple created with authority (“you shall,” 1:29), while 2:4ff. draws our attention to a primal couple created under authority (“you shall not,” 2:17)."

### C-V1R1-18 | Structure — colophons: ANE parallel but *tôlĕdôt* still introductory
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Some identify the formulae as colophons; ANE colophons (Hunger 563 Akkadian; Ugaritic; some OT “these are…” summaries) typically stand at the end; nonetheless Hamilton reads Genesis *tôlĕdôt* as introductory titles (majority view), not summarizing conclusions (Wiseman/Harrison minority).

### C-V1R1-19 | Structure — critique of Wiseman-Harrison eleven-tablet theory
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Wiseman and R. K. Harrison propose eleven literary units/tablets with *tôlĕdôt* as conclusions (e.g., 1:1–2:4 cosmos; 2:5–5:2 Adam…; Joseph appended); Hamilton finds this problematic: (1) where formula precedes genealogy it is hard not to include it with what follows; (2) it oddly makes Ishmael preserve Abraham’s history, etc.; (3) *tôlĕdôt* from *yālaḏ* must refer to what is born/produced—the historical result—so genitive is starting point, *tôlĕdôt* the result.
- **Quote:** "The proposal of Wiseman and Harrison has several problems. … A third problem is this view’s interpretation of the Hebrew word tôleḏôṯ. The noun comes from the verb yālaḏ (“to father, give birth to, bear”), and must refer to that which is born, or produced, that is, the historical result."
- **Locus:** slice L155–189 / raw L375–409
- **Targets:** [[toledot]], [[genesis]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R1-20 | Structure — literary-theological unity via focusing on key progeny
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Each *tôlĕdôt* focuses on one personality and weeds out lesser individuals (cosmos→Adam/Eve; Noah→Shem; Shem→Terah; Terah→Abram; Isaac→Jacob; Jacob→Joseph); absence of “generation of Abraham” or “of Joseph” shows these are not biographies but movement from progenitor to progeny implementing God’s plan—evidence of literary and theological unity.
- **Quote:** "the tôleḏôṯ structure of Genesis suggests a movement from a starting point to a finishing point, from a cause to an effect, from a progenitor to a progeny who is the key individual at that point in either implementing or perpetuating God’s plan and will in his heavens and earth."
- **Locus:** slice L189 / raw L409
- **Targets:** [[toledot]], [[genesis]], [[abraham]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R1-21 | Structure — geographical design Babylonia / Palestine / Egypt
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Gen 1–11 set in Babylonia; 12–36 in Palestine; 37–50 in Egypt; center (12–36) bracketed by regions with whose history Israel would be interlocked—impact: Genesis is about world history; Abraham elected so nations might find knowledge of God and blessing.
- **Quote:** "Chapters 1-11 are set in Babylonia; chs. 12-36 are set in Palestine; chs. 37-50 are set in Egypt. … The ultimate reason for the election of Abraham is that the nations of the earth … might find the knowledge of God and his blessing."
- **Locus:** slice L191 / raw L411

### C-V1R1-22 | Structure — primeval vs patriarchal history; land lost vs land sought
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Clear division at chs. 11/12: primeval history (1–11) vs patriarchal history (12–50); 1–11 individuals have land and lose/are expelled; 12–50 lack land and move toward it; four-fifths of Genesis on four generations (Abraham–Joseph) vs one-fifth on twenty (Adam–Abraham).
- **Quote:** "In chs. 1-11 we read of individuals who had land, but are either losing it or being expelled from it. In chs. 12-50 the emphasis is on individuals who do not have land, but are on the way toward it."

### C-V1R1-23 | Structure/Theology arc — generation → degeneration → regeneration
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** After 1–11’s increasing alienation (von Rad) or variety of alienation without crescendo (Westermann), chs. 12ff. are meant as solution; Abraham’s obedient model contrasts sorry models before him; covenant with humankind (Gen 8–9) is augmented by covenant with a family; Genesis moves from generation (1–2) to degeneration (3–11) to regeneration (12–50).
- **Quote:** "Genesis is moving us progressively from generation (chs. 1-2), to degeneration (chs. 3-11), to regeneration (chs. 12-50)."

### C-V1R1-24 | Composition — two millennia of unity/Mosaic assumption
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** For almost eighteen hundred years rabbinic and ecclesiastical scholars (Maimonides, Augustine, Calvin) agreed Genesis was a unified work of Moses; modern “precritical” label often unfairly sidelines their insights.
- **Quote:** "For almost eighteen hundred years (the first cycle) hardly anyone questioned the unity of Genesis… Thus a Maimonides within Judaism, an Augustine within Catholicism, and a Calvin within Protestantism shared no disagreement… Genesis was a unified work, and more specifically, the work of Moses."

### C-V1R1-25 | Composition — Astruc: divine names; Moses as redactor of sources
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Second cycle (~two centuries) begins with Jean Astruc: distribution of divine names led him to conclude Moses redacted Gen 1–Exod 2 from two primary parallel sources (Yahweh / Elohim) plus ten fragments, all pre-Mosaic—an orthodox measured response, not demolitionism.
- **Quote:** "His conclusion was that Moses was the redactor (not the author) of Gen. 1-Exod. 2, and that Moses collated two primary, parallel sources (one of which referred to the deity as “Yahweh,” and the other referred to the deity as “Elohim”), plus ten other fragments."
- **Locus:** slice L213 / raw L433

### C-V1R1-26 | Composition — Wellhausen’s four-source model (JEDP) summarized
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Consensus identifies four strands: J (Yahwist; Wellhausen ~850 BC; post-Wellhausen often 960–930 BC, Solomonic Judah); E (Elohist, ~850 BC, northern Israel, starts with patriarchs not creation); D (Deuteronomy, by Josianic reform ~620 BC or older, northern); P (Priestly, 550–450 BC; Wellhausen shifted P from earliest to latest; concerned with sacral institutions via history).
- **Quote:** "this approach identifies four major literary strands behind the present canonical shape of the Pentateuch. In chronological order these are:1. The Yahwist (J)… 2. The Elohist (E)… 3. Deuteronomy (D)… 4. The Priestly Writer (P) (550-450 B.C.)"
- **Locus:** slice L220–233 / raw L440–453
- **Targets:** [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[genesis]]

### C-V1R1-27 | Composition — classic criteria for multiple sources
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Reasons for multi-traditional Pentateuch, in descending significance: (1) different names for God; (2) irreconcilable duplications (two creations, meshed flood, two Abraham covenants chs. 15 & 17, two Hagar banishments, etc.); (3) anachronisms (Ur of the Chaldeans, Philistines, camels, Edomite kings list); (4) distinctive styles/ideologies (P formal/repetitious; J anthropomorphic direct contact; E dreams/angels).
- **Quote:** "There are a number of reasons for positing the existence of a multi-traditional Pentateuch. In descending order of significance, they are: (1) The different names for God. … (2) The presence of duplications… (3) The presence of anachronisms… (4) The detection in Genesis of distinctive literary styles or religious ideology"
- **Locus:** slice L242–248 / raw L462–468

### C-V1R1-28 | Composition — JEP distribution in Genesis
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Genesis is JEP (D confined to Deuteronomy); in 11:27–50:26 J predominates (730 vv J, 336 E, 153 P); E absent from primeval history, first connected narrative contribution not until ch. 20; P as narrative only sparingly in four passages (1:1–2:4a; 6:1–9:29; 17:1–27; 23:1–20), major contribution genealogies and framework of numbers/dates/years.

- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Noth amalgamated short oral units into larger complexes around five Pentateuch themes; only the patriarchal theme (promise of land and prosperity to Abraham, then Isaac and Jacob) is in Genesis; Abraham/Isaac/Jacob historical as figures but little in Genesis about them historical because stories originated in different places/clans.

### C-V1R1-77 | Hebrew text — MT/LXX minor differences; chronology chs. 5, 8, 11 most serious
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** MT and LXX differ only minorly: contextual harmonization (2:2 seventh→sixth day); d/r confusion (22:13; 3:17; 8:21); rare→common words (15:11 *nāšaḇ*/*yāšaḇ*; 49:10 Shiloh; 26:20 Esek); occasional LXX plus (35:22); most serious difference is chronological systems in chs. 5, 8, 11 (LXX partially with SP).
- **Quote:** "The MT and LXX have only minor differences in Genesis. … (5) The most serious difference between the MT and LXX is the chronological system in chs. 5, 8, 11. The LXX partially agrees with the SP."
- **Locus:** slice L814 / raw L1034
- **Targets:** [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]
